article.description: El hielo cerca de la cumbre del pico montañoso indonesio se ha reducido a parches dispersos demasiado pequeños para fluir como glaciares.
article.explanation:
**El último hielo en el Puncak Jaya**

El Puncak Jaya, ubicado en la cordillera Sudirman de Indonesia, ha sido uno de los pocos lugares cerca del ecuador donde el hielo ha persistido durante todo el año. Sin embargo, las imágenes satelitales muestran una alarmante reducción de sus glaciares. En 1988, estos cubrían aproximadamente 4.31 kilómetros cuadrados, mientras que para septiembre de 2025, solo quedaban alrededor de 0.09 kilómetros cuadrados, lo que representa cerca del 2% de su extensión original.

El espesor del hielo también ha disminuido drásticamente. En 2010, el hielo en el sitio de monitoreo principal tenía una altura de 32 metros, pero para 2023, este se redujo a solo 4 metros. Este proceso de adelgazamiento ha llevado a que los glaciares se fragmenten, creando bordes expuestos que aceleran el derretimiento.

Los científicos advierten que, debido a las condiciones climáticas actuales y fenómenos como El Niño, la desaparición total de estos glaciares podría ocurrir alrededor de 2030. Durante eventos de El Niño pasados, el hielo se ha derretido a un ritmo alarmante, lo que subraya la vulnerabilidad de estas masas de hielo en un clima cambiante.

Bare rock appears brown, and glacial ice, shown in blue, caps several of the highest ridges. Vegetation at lower elevations appears green. NASA Earth Observatory / Lauren Dauphin A false-color satellite image shows the same area in 2026. Only a few small fragments of ice remain, shown in blue, and bare brown rock covers most of the ridgetops that were icy in 1988. NASA Earth Observatory / Lauren Dauphin 1988 2026 A false-color satellite image from 1988 shows mountain ridges of Indonesia’s Sudirman Range. Bare rock appears brown, and glacial ice, shown in blue, caps several of the highest ridges. Vegetation at lower elevations appears green. NASA Earth Observatory / Lauren Dauphin A false-color satellite image shows the same area in 2026. Only a few small fragments of ice remain, shown in blue, and bare brown rock covers most of the ridgetops that were icy in 1988. NASA Earth Observatory / Lauren Dauphin 1988 2026 Curtain Toggle 2-Up On the island of New Guinea, Indonesia’s Sudirman Range is one of the few places near the equator that have long held ice year-round. But near the summit of Puncak Jaya, the ice has dwindled to patches too small to flow like glaciers. Positioned in the tropics beside the largest expanse of warm ocean water on Earth, the range’s glaciers lie near the warmest conditions in which ice can survive year-round. Scientists have described these glaciers as high-altitude “ canaries in the coal mine ,” alongside other tropical ice such as the remnants of Humboldt Glacier in Venezuela, Quelccaya Ice Cap in Peru, and the ice fields of Kilimanjaro in Tanzania. The change on Puncak Jaya is visible in this image pair, acquired in 1988 by the TM (Thematic Mapper) on Landsat 5 (left) and in 2026 by the OLI (Operational Land Imager) on Landsat 9 (right). The false-color images help distinguish areas of ice (light blue) from exposed bedrock (brown). Clouds appear white and vegetation green. In 1988, the glaciers covered about 4.31 square kilometers (1.66 square miles), according to Donaldi Permana, a climate scientist at the Indonesian Agency for Meteorology, Climatology, and Geophysics ( BMKG ). By September 2025, satellite and aerial data showed that only about 0.09 square kilometers (0.03 square miles) remained—an area equivalent to about a dozen soccer fields. That’s roughly 2 percent of the 1988 extent . An aerial survey planned for December should yield an estimate of how much ice remains in 2026, Permana said. The glaciers have thinned, too. Measurements at the primary monitoring site on the East Northwall Firn showed a drop from 32 meters (105 feet) thick in 2010 to 4 meters (13 feet) in 2023, Permana said. By November 2024, the ice at this site was gone. As the glaciers thin, they also break apart, and each new fragment adds exposed edges where ice can melt, compounding the losses. In the 2026 Landsat image, freshly uncovered bedrock appears between the remnants. Snow still falls in the area, but it doesn’t last long enough on the bare rock to build up into new ice. “It’s a house of cards problem,” said Chris Shuman, a retired University of Maryland glaciologist who has tracked Puncak Jaya’s glaciers in satellite imagery. “Once this process gets going, there’s really no turning back.” To qualify as a glacier, a body of ice generally has to be thick enough to flow downhill under its own weight, and it needs an area where snow builds up faster than it melts. Puncak Jaya’s remaining ice has thinned so much and broken into such small, stagnant patches that it no longer flows. “While small ice remnants persist in high-altitude crevices around Puncak Jaya, their functional life as active glaciers is effectively over,” Permana said. As for the remaining patches of ice, time will tell how long they last. Recent satellite studies suggest complete disappearance of the main glacial ice areas could occur around 2030. Permana noted that BMKG estimates suggest they could be gone much sooner, hastened by the current El Niño . Past El Niño years have hit these glaciers especially hard. As the air warms, the freezing level rises above the summit, so precipitation falls as rain instead of snow. That means less fresh white snow that normally reflects sunlight and shields the ice, leaving darker surfaces that absorb more heat and melt faster. During the 2015-2016 El Niño, the ice thinned about five times faster than usual , losing roughly 5.3 meters (17 feet) of thickness in a single year. The 2023-2024 El Niño brought another bout of rapid thinning, about 2 to 4 meters (7 to 13 feet) per year. article.explanation: 1 Min Leer Un collage que muestra 49 agujeros de perforación realizados por el rover Curiosity de Marte de NASA PIA26802 Créditos: NASA/JPL-Caltech/MSSS Fotojournal Navegación Fotojournal Un collage que muestra 49 agujeros de perforación… Fotojournal Inicio Fotojournal Buscar Contenido más reciente Galerías Comentarios RSS Acerca de Descargas Un collage que muestra 49 agujeros de perforación realizados por el rover Curiosity de Marte de NASA JPEG (13.80 MB) Descripción Este collage muestra 49 agujeros de perforación capturados por el rover Curiosity de Marte de NASA hasta noviembre de 2026. Cada agujero representa una muestra recolectada de rocas en la superficie marciana; el taladro de Curiosity, ubicado en el extremo de su brazo robótico, deja caer muestras de roca pulverizada en instrumentos en su interior que analizan su composición. Estas imágenes fueron tomadas por el Mars Hand Lens Imager (MAHLI), una cámara que también se encuentra en el extremo del brazo robótico del rover. Cada agujero tiene un diámetro de 0.63 pulgadas (16 milímetros). Curiosity fue construido por el Laboratorio de Propulsión a Chorro de NASA, que es administrado por Caltech en Pasadena, California. JPL lidera la misión en nombre de la Dirección de Misiones Científicas de NASA en Washington como parte del portafolio del Programa de Exploración de Marte de NASA.

article.original_title: A Collage Showing 49 Drill Holes Made by NASA’s Curiosity Mars Rover
article.source_body: 1 Min Read A Collage Showing 49 Drill Holes Made by NASA’s Curiosity Mars Rover PIA26802 Credits: NASA/JPL-Caltech/MSSS Photojournal Navigation Science Photojournal A Collage Showing 49 Drill… Photojournal Home Photojournal Search Latest Content Galleries Feedback RSS About Downloads A Collage Showing 49 Drill Holes Made by NASA’s Curiosity Mars Rover JPEG (13.80 MB) Description This collage shows 49 drill holes captured by NASA’s Curiosity Mars rover as of November 2026. Each hole represents a sample collected from rocks on the Martian surface; Curiosity’s drill, located on the end of its robotic arm, drops pulverized rock samples into instruments in its belly that analyze their composition. These images were taken by the Mars Hand Lens Imager (MAHLI), a camera that is also located on the end of the rover’s robotic arm. Each hole has a diameter of 0.63 inches (16 millimeters). Curiosity was built by NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory, which is managed by Caltech in Pasadena, California. JPL leads the mission on behalf of NASA’s Science Mission Directorate in Washington as part of NASA’s Mars Exploration Program portfolio. MAHLI was built by Malin Space Science Systems in San Diego.
